paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Empirical probability, also called experimental probability, is an estimate of how likely an event is. It comes from an actual sample of observations rather than from a theoretical sample space. More broadly, it can be estimated from experience and observation.

paragraphs.heading: How to work it out
paragraphs.text: The usual way to estimate it is the relative frequency. Count how many times the event was recorded, then divide by the total number of trials. In symbols, if an event A in a sample space happens in m outcomes out of n outcomes in all, its relative frequency is m/n.

paragraphs.heading: Strength: few assumptions
paragraphs.text: One advantage of this approach is that it rests on relatively few assumptions. Suppose you want the chance that a man is over 6 feet tall and also prefers strawberry jam to raspberry jam. You could simply count the men who meet both conditions. Another route would multiply the share of men over 6 feet by the share who prefer strawberry jam, but that estimate depends on assuming the two traits are statistically independent.

paragraphs.heading: Weakness: near-zero or near-one odds
paragraphs.text: Trouble comes with probabilities very close to zero or very close to one. Estimating those to a good standard of relative accuracy would need very large samples. Statistical models can help here, depending on the context, and may give better accuracy than empirical probabilities, as long as the assumptions behind them actually hold.

paragraphs.heading: Example: a freezing February
paragraphs.text: Suppose you want the probability that, at some site, the lowest of the daily-maximum temperatures in February of a given year drops below zero degrees Celsius. You could use the record of past years to estimate it. Alternatively, you could pick a family of probability distributions, fit it to the past values, and take the probability from the fitted distribution. The model route can give an answer even if every value in the record is above zero.

paragraphs.heading: Other names
paragraphs.text: It is sometimes called a-posteriori probability. That name echoes terms from Bayesian statistics, yet it has no direct link to Bayesian inference, where a similar-sounding term can mean posterior probability, which is a different thing. In the empirical sense, a-posteriori probability may be paired with a priori probability, an estimate built on deductive reasoning rather than on observations.
